opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the four parts are the policy, the value function, the perception or state representation, and then the transition model of the world. The transition model is your belief about what will happen if you do something. It's your model of the consequences of your actions. So it's the physics of the world, but it's not just physics. It's also more abstract models, like if I go to the airport, or if I say this to you, what's likely to happen next.

And the important thing is that this is learned, and it's learned richly from all the sensation you receive, not just from reward. Reward is a pretty small part of it. Most of what you're learning about the world is this predictive knowledge: when I do this, that tends to follow. You'd learn it from experience, just by acting and observing what happens, without anyone labeling anything for you.

Then that model is what you use for planning. You can imagine taking an action, see what the model says will follow, evaluate that with your value function, and that lets you improve your policy without actually having to try everything out in the real world. So the transition model is really the part that holds your understanding of how the world works, and I think it's going to be a very large part of what an intelligent agent knows, probably the bulk of its knowledge.

r001.rationale: It describes the transition model as a belief about what will happen when the agent acts and as a model of action consequences.

r002.rationale: It gives abstract examples beyond physical dynamics, such as going to the airport or saying something and predicting what follows.

r003.rationale: It says the model is learned through experience by acting and observing what happens.

r004.rationale: It says reward is a pretty small part of learning about the world, while most of that learning is predictive knowledge about what follows from actions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the four parts, as I think about them, are the policy, the value function, the perception component, and the transition model of the world. The first two are the ones people usually focus on in reinforcement learning, and the perception part is about forming your state representation, your sense of where you are. The transition model is the fourth, and in some ways it's the most ambitious, because it's the agent's knowledge of the physics of its world. It's a prediction of what will happen if I do this. If I take this action in this state, what state will I end up in, and what reward will I get?

I like to think of it as the agent's beliefs about how the world works. And the important thing is that it's learned from experience. It's not given to the agent by a designer who already knows the dynamics. The agent acts, it sees what follows, and it adjusts its model to predict those consequences better. Then the model is used for planning. Planning, to me, is just the process of using the model to improve the policy and value function without having to actually take the actions in the world. You imagine, you try things out in your head, and you learn from the imagined experience. That's what Dyna was about, going back to the early nineties, and I still think that's the right basic picture.

What makes it hard is that the world is enormous and the agent is small. You can't model everything, and you shouldn't try. So the model has to be abstract. It has to be in terms of the agent's own state representation, in terms of features, not raw pixels. And it has to be temporally abstract, so you can predict what happens if you pursue a course of action for a while, not just what happens at the next time step. That's where options come in. Those are the pieces I think we still haven't gotten right, and I'd say that learning a good transition model from experience, at the right level of abstraction, is probably the most important open problem in AI.

r001.rationale: It says the model predicts what happens after an action, including the resulting state and reward.

r002.rationale: It describes feature-based and temporally abstract modeling, but does not state that the model represents transitions beyond physical dynamics.

r003.rationale: It says the agent acts, observes what follows, and adjusts its model to predict those consequences better.

r004.rationale: It includes reward among the predicted consequences, but does not say reward is only a small part of what the model represents.

astra-6.text:
The transition model is the part that predicts what happens next. If I’m in this state and I take this action, what state will I end up in, and what reward will I receive? It might predict a distribution of outcomes rather than a single outcome.

That’s different from the policy, which tells you what action to take, and the value function, which tells you how much reward you can expect over the longer run. The model lets you consider possible actions before actually taking them. You can imagine taking an action, predict the resulting state, and then use your value function to evaluate that state. That’s how the model supports planning.

And it doesn’t have to be a complete model of the world. It needs to capture the aspects of the world that are useful for predicting the consequences of your actions.

r001.rationale: It says the model predicts what state and reward follow from taking an action, and that it predicts action consequences.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting states and rewards but does not say the model can represent abstract transitions beyond physical dynamics.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the agent learns the model by observing what happens after acting.

r004.rationale: It mentions predicted reward but does not characterize reward as only a small part of what the model represents.

sol-6.1.text:
The transition model is the part that predicts what happens next. If I’m in a particular state and take a particular action, what will the next state be, and what reward will I receive? It might predict a distribution over those possibilities rather than one definite outcome.

That’s different from the policy, which tells you what action to take, and the value function, which tells you how much reward you can expect over the longer term. The model lets you consider an action without actually taking it. You can use it to generate hypothetical experience, and then learn from that experience much as you would learn from interaction with the world. That’s planning.

And it needn’t be a model of everything in the world. It needs to predict the aspects of the world that matter for the agent’s decisions.

r001.rationale: It says the model predicts the next state and reward given a state and action.

r002.rationale: It says the model need only predict decision-relevant aspects, but does not state that transitions can be abstract rather than physical.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from hypothetical experience generated by the model, not learning the model by observing what happens after acting.

r004.rationale: It mentions predicting reward but does not say reward is only a small part of what the model represents.
